Paci non pactis sed poenis (legibus = legibus poenalibus) providendum — “Peace and security must therefore be secured not through agreements but through punishments.” Hobbes, M/B, p. 133.
Who is so stupid that he cannot see the fraud? And who so bold that he will say he sees it? — Shakespeare, King Richard III, Act III, Scene 6.

Bachofen turns Epimetheus into a dull hylic man — See Johann Jacob Bachofen, Der Mythus von Orient und Occident. Eine Metaphysik der Alten Welt, with an introduction by Alfred Baeumler, ed. Manfred Schroeter, Munich 1926, pp. 318–319. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 24846.
Carl Spitteler — (1845–1924), Swiss poet and author of the epic Prometheus und Epimetheus.

“the need of the person who acts to appear” — Max Kommerell, Schiller als Gestalter des handelnden Menschen. Gedenkrede gehalten in der Universität Bonn am 9. November 1934 (Wissenschaft und Gegenwart, 6), Frankfurt am Main 1934, p. 20. Schmitt’s annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 27868.

“like a prostitute in a tavern” — “The German people hailed and worshipped their National Assembly of 1848 like a goddess of freedom, only to let it perish one year later ‘like a prostitute in a tavern’—such was the judgment of the Spanish diplomat Donoso Cortés in his speech on the general situation in Europe on 30 January 1850.”
Veit Valentin, Geschichte der deutschen Revolution von 1848–49, Berlin 1930–1931, vol. 2, p. 1.
“Yet he is not the son of my heart …” — F. Schiller, Demetrius, Act II, Scene 1. Correctly: “Yet even if he were …”
the coinage “discriminating concept of war” — C. Schmitt, Die Wendung zum diskriminierenden Kriegsbegriff, Munich/Leipzig 1938; annotated reprint in FoP, pp. 518–597.
Kommerell’s lecture — See Max Kommerell, Schiller als Gestalter des handelnden Menschen. Gedenkrede gehalten in der Universität Bonn am 9. November 1934, Frankfurt am Main 1934, pp. 15–16.
**Erich Voegelin’s Rassenidee*** — Erich Voegelin, *Die Rassenidee in der Geistesgeschichte von Ray bis Carus, Berlin 1933. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 25790.
Churchill’s speech — In a speech to the House of Commons on 21 April 1944, Churchill said: “In a world of confusion and ruin the old flag flies.”
Schmitt was in Portugal from 13 to 23 May 1944, so he cannot have heard the speech there.

“Et le vent furibond de la concupiscence …” — From Charles Baudelaire’s poem “Femmes damnées” in the collection L’Épaves. In Baudelaire, Sämtliche Werke/Briefe, ed. Friedhelm Kemp and Claude Pichois, vol. 4, Munich/Vienna 1975, pp. 14 ff.
Sussmann’s requiem for Däubler — Toni Sussmann, Theodor Däubler. Ein Requiem, edition prepared by Jakob Hegner, London 1948. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 28651.
Toni Sussmann (1884–1967), a friend and ardent admirer of Däubler, regarded herself after his death as his “spiritual widow.” She was also friends with Jakob Hegner. See BW Mohler, p. 28.
Hans Fleig obtained the book for Schmitt; see ibid., p. 56.
Günther Anders — (1902–1992), born Günther Siegmund Stern, philosopher and writer.
to publish it with Suhrkamp, 1949 — See Günther Anders, Über Heidegger, Munich 2001, p. 69.
Kafka essay by the same author — Günther Anders, “Kafka — Pro und Kontra. Die Prozeßunterlagen,” in Neue Rundschau 58, 1947, pp. 119–157. Also published separately, Munich 1951 and in later editions.
Asinus mysteria vehens — “A donkey carrying mysteries.” The expression, which goes back to a comedy by Aristophanes or to the Metamorphoses of Apuleius, became proverbial.
Êtes-vous heureux? … — From the French version of Lord Byron’s drama Cain:
“Cain: Are you happy? Lucifer: We are powerful.”
Act I, Scene 1. On Byron, see PR, p. 27.

miracle of the Deutsche Mark: Thomas Mann appears in Germany again — Thomas Mann hesitated for a long time before returning to Europe after the war. On his first European journey, in 1947, he visited England, the Netherlands, and Switzerland. Two years later he travelled through England, Sweden, Denmark, and Switzerland and also entered Germany, where in Frankfurt he received the Goethe Prize, worth DM 10,000.
“In many deaths, one guilt dies here …” — Max Kommerell, Die Gefangenen. Trauerspiel in 5 Akten, Frankfurt am Main 1948, p. 9.
δός μοι ποῦ στῶ — See the note above on p. 40.
We have nothing with which we can compare it — Goethe, Torquato Tasso, Act V, Scene 5, Hamburg edition, vol. 5, p. 162.

Jesus is the Christ — Hobbes quotes the Bible with this sentence in Leviathan, chapter 43, referring to Acts 17:3. See BdP, pp. 121–122; C. Schmitt, “Die vollendete Reformation,” in Leviathan, pp. [163] ff.
Between Stalin organs … — Modelled on Friedrich Schiller’s poem “Das Ideal und das Leben,” whose first stanza reads:
“Between sensual happiness and peace of soul Man is left with only the anxious choice; Upon the forehead of the lofty Uranid Their united radiance shines.”
The idea has always disgraced itself in such cases, Friedrich Engels said — Not Engels, but Marx:
“The ‘Idea’ always disgraced itself insofar as it was separated from ‘Interest.’”
Karl Marx, Die Heilige Familie, in Marx, Die Frühschriften, ed. S. Landshut, Stuttgart 1953, p. 320.
Qui n’a pas l’esprit de son âge, de son âge a tout le malheur — “Anyone who does not possess the spirit of his age suffers all the misfortunes of his age.” Voltaire, Stances, VIII, 11–12.
homo verbo fit potentior — Thomas Hobbes, De homine, chapter X.3:

Denique propter loquendi facilitate Homo quae ne cogitate quidem loquitur, & quae loquitur credit vera esse, & se ipsum decipere potest; Bestia se ipsam fallere non potest. Itaque Oratione Homo non melior fit sed potentior.

“Finally, because speech comes so easily, human beings are led to speak even when they are not thinking at all; and by believing that what they say is true, they can deceive themselves. An animal cannot deceive itself. Through language, therefore, a human being becomes not better, but more powerful.”
gens prophetarum avida — Thomas Hobbes, De cive, chapter XVI.15:

Potestas itaque civilis summa debebatur jure, ex institutione Dei, Sacerdoti summo. Facto autem potestas illa in Prophetis erat, quibus (a Deo extraordinarie suscitatis) Israelitae (gens Prophetarum avida) propter existimationem prophetiae protegendos se & judicandos subjecerunt.

“By God’s own institution, therefore, the highest civil power belonged by right to the High Priest. In practice, however, this power was held by the prophets, to whom the Israelites—a people eager for prophets—submitted themselves for protection and judgment because of the authority they attributed to prophecy, these prophets having been raised up by God in an extraordinary way.”
non enim potest civis privatim determinare … — Correctly:
non potest civis quisquam privatim determinare, quis sit amicus, vel quis hostis publicus, quando bellum, quando foedus, quando pax, quando induciae ineundae sint;
“No private citizen may decide for himself who is to count as the state’s friend or public enemy, when war is to begin, when an alliance is to be made, or when peace or a truce is to be concluded.”
Homer Lea — (1876–1912), American geopolitical writer. His final book, The Day of the Saxon, predicted the fall of the British Empire in 1912.
“This peace is beginning to annoy me” — Quotation from Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht (Geneva edition), vol. 2, Leipzig 1922: “Der Ararat, Die Apokalypse,” p. 487.
written to Mrs. Jünger — Not included in the published edition of the correspondence, BW GJ.

Estrada Doctrine and Bogotá Charter — The Estrada Doctrine, named after Mexican Foreign Minister J. V. Estrada and formulated in 1930, held that either recognizing or refusing to recognize a foreign government amounts to interference in its internal affairs and should therefore be avoided.
The Bogotá Charter was an international agreement concluded in 1948 among several American states, under which they committed themselves to resolving conflicts among themselves without violence.

**Hegel, addition to § 70 of the *Philosophy of Right*** — Hegel here denies that a person has a property right over his own personality and therefore rejects suicide. The same applies to the “conduct of the hero” who throws himself on his own sword.
Sic Baader — Franz von Baader to Professor Hoffmann, 6 September 1835. In F. von Baader, Sämtliche Werke, ed. Franz Hoffmann and others, vol. 15 (= Nachgelassene Werke, vol. 5), Leipzig 1857, p. 528.
the impostor Lüth — Paul Lüth (1921–1986), who presented himself as a doctor despite not having completed his medical studies; author of writings on literary history and newspaper essays.

Mahan — Alfred Thayer Mahan (1840–1914), American rear admiral and naval writer, an intellectual representative of US imperialism; his most important work was The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890). See Maschke’s note in SGN, pp. 327–328 and 437.
“For Ahasuerus, who in 1933 …” — Ernst Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 8, p. 102.

Hans Paeschke — (1911–1991), journalist and publisher. In 1947 he founded the monthly journal Merkur with Joachim Moras and remained its editor until 1978. Paeschke visited Schmitt in Plettenberg in July 1949; see his letters to Schmitt, RW 265, nos. 10756–10781.
Karl Löwith — (1897–1973), philosopher. Löwith emigrated in 1934 and, under the pseudonym “Hugo Fiala,” launched a sharp attack on Schmitt in 1935.

Schmitt responded to Löwith in 1944 in “Donoso Cortés in gesamteuropäischer Interpretation,” criticizing the fact that Löwith, in his book Von Hegel zu Nietzsche, “leaves essential questions in Bruno Bauer entirely out of account.” C. Schmitt, Donoso Cortés in gesamteuropäischer Interpretation, Cologne 1950, p. 99.
Löwith later acknowledged to Hanno Kesting that this criticism was justified. See H. Kesting’s letter to Schmitt of 22 September 1950, RW 265, no. 7467.

Schmitt also engaged with Löwith in his review of Meaning in History: C. Schmitt, “Drei Stufen historischer Sinngebung,” in Universitas 5, 1950, pp. 927–931. Under its original title, “Drei Möglichkeiten eines christlichen Geschichtsbildes,” it was reprinted in BW Blumenberg, pp. 161–166.

Schmitt gave the manuscript to Merkur editor Paeschke to read and suggested that he send it to Löwith without naming its author. Paeschke did so. The relevant letter survives in the papers of the Merkur editorial office at the German Literature Archive, HS 2274096.
For a German translation of Löwith’s book, Schmitt proposed Hanno Kesting, who completed it with substantial assistance from Reinhart Koselleck.
non possum scribere de eo qui potest proscibere — Correctly:
non est enim facile in eum scribere qui potest proscribere.
“It is not easy to write against someone who has the power to put you on a proscription list.”
Schmitt had already been fond of citing this sentence during the Nazi period—for example to Ernst Jünger; see Jünger’s Strahlungen, in E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 2, p. 265.

Viennese émigré named Karpfen — Otto Maria Carpeaux, originally Otto Karpfen (1900–1978), Austrian journalist and literary critic. He converted from Judaism to Catholicism in 1932 and added “Maria” to his name. After the annexation of Austria he was forced into exile in Brazil, where he changed his name to Carpeaux.
See Mauro Souza Ventura, De Karpfen a Carpeaux. Formação política e interpretação literária na obra do crítico austríaco-brasileiro, Rio de Janeiro 2002.

On his dispute with Bernanos, see Andreas Pfersmann, “Carpeaux versus Bernanos. Eine literar. Fehde im brasilian. Exil,” in Gilbert Ravy, ed., Nouvelles recherches sur l’Autriche (Austriaca, 36), Rouen 1993.

Isidore Isou — Ioan-Isidor Goldstein (1925–2007), Romanian scandal-writer, artist, and philosopher who lived in France from 1945 onward and called himself Isidore Isou. His book L’Agrégation d’un nom et d’un messie, published by Gallimard in 1947, is an autobiographical novel.
“Not willed, only faithful …” — From a poem by Konrad Weiß. In Weiß, p. 549:
“Deeply astonished, full of awe, I see how everything falls into place; nothing betrays me, not willed, only faithfully followed, […]”

Bach is musical oratory — Arnold Schmitz (1893–1980), music historian and close friend of Carl Schmitt since 1922, had worked on this subject—for example in “Die Oratorische Kunst J. S. Bachs. Grundfragen und Grundlagen,” Kongreßbericht. Gesellschaft für Musikforschung. Lüneburg 1950, pp. 33–49; reprinted in Walter Blankenburg, ed., Johann Sebastian Bach, Darmstadt 1970, pp. 61–84.
Schmitz sent Schmitt an offprint bearing the dedication: “To Carl Schmitt, with respect, admiration, friendship, and gratitude — Arnold Schmitz.” The copy remains in private hands.

For decades the two men had discussed the specifically Western tradition of music tied to words. Arnold Schmitz’s monograph Die Bildlichkeit der wortgebundenen Musik Johann Sebastian Bachs, Mainz 1950, appeared with a printed dedication to Carl Schmitt.
Donnedieu de Vabres — Henri Donnedieu de Vabres (1880–1952), French lawyer and judge at the Nuremberg trials.
the Horkia — τὰ ὅρκια, the sacred rites connected with the taking of a solemn oath, especially in Homer.
Tell it to no one but the wise — Correctly: “Tell it to no one, only to the wise.” Goethe, West-östlicher Divan, poem “Selige Sehnsucht,” Hamburg edition, vol. 2, pp. 18–19.
Maxima non curat praetor — Properly: Minima non curat praetor, “The praetor does not concern himself with trivial matters.” A maxim from Roman law.

the force with which Werner Weber criticizes the work — Werner Weber (1904–1976), a student of Schmitt and, from 1949 onward, professor of public and constitutional law at Göttingen. Between 1949 and 1951 he published three essays criticizing the Bonn Basic Law. They were later collected in W. Weber, Spannungen und Kräfte im westdeutschen Verfassungssystem, Stuttgart 1951.

Bella gerant alii — Bella gerant alii, tu, felix Austria, nube! “Let others wage wars; you, happy Austria, marry!” A couplet by an anonymous poet referring to the successful marriage policy of Maximilian I.
**Kempner in Der Monat*** — Robert M. W. Kempner, “Der Kampf gegen die Kirche. Aus unveröffentlichten Tagebüchern Alfred Rosenbergs,” in *Der Monat 1, 1949, pp. 26–38.

Rosenberg’s diaries from the years 1934 to 1944 were believed to have disappeared after 1945. In fact, Robert Kempner had possession of the manuscript and took it with him to the United States. It was not rediscovered until 2013 and was published in 2015: A. Rosenberg, Die Tagebücher von 1934 bis 1944, ed. Jürgen Matthäus and Frank Bajohr, Frankfurt am Main 2015.
